meta.name: Splunk Enterprise Certified Admin
meta.notes: [initial seed pack — 12 questions covering distributed components, forwarders, indexer/search-head clustering, license manager, bucket lifecycle, inputs.conf/props.conf precedence, deployment server] | v1.1 (2026-07-03): +10 scenario questions — RF vs SF, deployment server/serverclass, props.conf index-time parsing, conf precedence, bucket lifecycle, props+transforms routing, license violations, SHC deployer bundle, delete capability RBAC, Monitoring Console. Balanced correct positions.

questions.question: Which Splunk Enterprise component is responsible for parsing incoming data, writing events to indexes on disk, and answering search requests from a search head?
questions.explanation: The indexer parses incoming data into events, writes them to indexes on disk in bucket directories, and returns matching events to search heads during distributed search. Universal forwarders only collect and forward data (no parsing). The deployment server distributes apps and configurations to forwarders. The license manager tracks daily ingest volume against the license pool.

questions.question: A customer wants to forward syslog data from 500 endpoints to Splunk with the smallest possible CPU and memory footprint on each endpoint. Which forwarder type is the correct choice?
questions.explanation: The universal forwarder is a dedicated, lightweight agent — it has no UI, no search capability, and minimal parsing — designed precisely for low-overhead data collection at scale. A heavy forwarder is a full Splunk Enterprise install used when local parsing, routing rules, or filtering is required. HEC is a token-authenticated HTTP endpoint for applications, not a host agent. "Search head forwarder cluster" is not a real component.

questions.question: On an indexer cluster, what does a replication factor (RF) of 3 and a search factor (SF) of 2 mean?
options: Each bucket has 3 raw copies and 2 of those copies are searchable (include indexed files like .tsidx)
The cluster keeps 3 days of hot buckets and 2 days of warm buckets
Each event is duplicated 3 times in the index and 2 of those are visible to users
questions.explanation: In an indexer cluster the replication factor (RF) is the number of complete bucket copies maintained across peer nodes — this protects raw data. The search factor (SF) is the number of those copies that are also kept as searchable copies (with `.tsidx` index files); SF must be ≤ RF. With RF=3/SF=2 the cluster tolerates two peer-node failures without data loss and one peer-node failure without losing immediate searchability. RF/SF describe bucket copies, not search-head counts, hot/warm retention, or event duplication.

questions.question: An admin needs to push a single set of inputs.conf and outputs.conf changes to 200 universal forwarders. Which Splunk role centrally manages and deploys these app bundles?
questions.explanation: The deployment server centrally distributes apps and configuration bundles to deployment clients (typically universal forwarders), grouped by `serverclass.conf` definitions that match clients by host, IP, DNS, or client name. The cluster manager (formerly master node) coordinates an indexer cluster, not forwarders. The license manager only meters ingestion. The Monitoring Console is a read-only health dashboard.

questions.question: An administrator is planning storage tiers and retention for an index and needs to know how a bucket ages from the moment data is first written until it is removed. In Splunk Enterprise, what is the correct lifecycle order for an index bucket from creation to deletion?
options: Hot → warm → cold → frozen (deleted or archived)
questions.explanation: Buckets are created as hot (open and writable on the indexer's fastest storage), rolled to warm when they reach size or time limits (closed, still on hot/warm volume), then rolled to cold storage (typically slower/cheaper disk), and finally frozen — at which point Splunk deletes them by default unless `coldToFrozenDir` or `coldToFrozenScript` is configured to archive. A thawed bucket is a frozen bucket re-imported for searching; it is not part of the normal forward lifecycle.

questions.question: An admin defines the same stanza `[monitor:///var/log/nginx/access.log]` in both `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/inputs.conf` and inside an app at `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/nginx_inputs/local/inputs.conf`. Which configuration wins for that input?
options: The app's local/inputs.conf (apps override system local)
Whichever file has the most recent modification time wins
The two settings are merged stanza-by-stanza with no winner
system/local/inputs.conf (system local has the highest precedence)
questions.explanation: Splunk's configuration file precedence (for input/index-time context) places `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/` above any app's `local/` directory. The precedence order is roughly: system/local > app/local > app/default > system/default. Modification time and "merge with no winner" are not how Splunk resolves conflicts — it picks one value per attribute based on precedence and lexical app order.

questions.question: Which Splunk configuration file is the correct place to assign a sourcetype to incoming events based on the file path, and to set line-breaking and timestamp-extraction rules for that sourcetype?
questions.explanation: `props.conf` is where source/sourcetype/host-based parsing rules live — including `LINE_BREAKER`, `SHOULD_LINEMERGE`, `TIME_PREFIX`, `TIME_FORMAT`, `MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD`, and `TRANSFORMS-*` references. `inputs.conf` only declares the data source (a monitor stanza, TCP port, scripted input, etc.). `outputs.conf` configures forwarder destinations. `transforms.conf` defines regex-based field extractions and routing rules that are invoked from `props.conf`.

questions.question: A Splunk environment ingests 480 GB on Monday against a 500 GB/day license. On Tuesday it ingests 540 GB. What happens?
options: Tuesday's ingest is hard-blocked at 500 GB and 40 GB is silently dropped
The Monday under-use of 20 GB carries forward and absorbs the Tuesday overage
The Splunk indexers stop accepting data immediately and forwarders queue indefinitely
A license violation is recorded; after 5 violations in a rolling 30-day window, search is disabled on affected indexes
questions.explanation: Splunk Enterprise records a license violation when daily indexed volume exceeds the licensed quota. With Enterprise (free trial and dev licenses behave differently) data continues to be indexed but a warning is logged; if 5 violations occur in a rolling 30-day window (the standard threshold), search is disabled on the affected indexes until the violation is cleared or a stacking license is added. Splunk does not silently drop, hard-block ingest, or carry over unused quota.

questions.question: In a search head cluster the members must stay in sync and elect a leader to schedule jobs and replicate configuration. Which component coordinates a search head cluster, including configuration replication and captaincy election among the members?
options: The deployer (separate Splunk instance, not part of the cluster)
Any one of the search heads, dynamically promoted
questions.explanation: A search head cluster (SHC) is managed by a dedicated **deployer** — a separate Splunk instance that bundles and pushes app and configuration updates to all SHC members. The cluster itself elects a **captain** (a member, not an external node) at runtime to coordinate replication and job scheduling; that's separate from the deployer's role. The cluster manager / master node is the indexer-cluster controller, a different cluster type. The deployment server manages forwarders, not search head clusters.

questions.question: On a heavy forwarder, an admin wants to route events from sourcetype `cisco:asa` to a remote indexer group while still indexing all other data locally. Which two configuration files are required to define this routing?
options: props.conf and transforms.conf (and outputs.conf to define the target group)
questions.explanation: Selective indexer routing on a heavy forwarder is driven by `props.conf` (which attaches a `TRANSFORMS-routing` to the sourcetype) plus `transforms.conf` (which defines a routing stanza with `DEST_KEY=_TCP_ROUTING` and `FORMAT=<target_group>`). The target group itself is defined in `outputs.conf`. `inputs.conf`/`indexes.conf` configure data collection and on-disk indexes, not routing. The `deploymentclient`/`serverclass` files manage deployment-server relationships. The `authentication`/`authorize` files configure auth and roles.

questions.question: Which Splunk role-based access mechanism controls whether a user can perform a specific action like running a real-time search, scheduling a search, or editing knowledge objects?
questions.explanation: Capabilities (such as `rtsearch`, `schedule_search`, `edit_user`, `delete_by_keyword`) are granular permissions defined per role in `authorize.conf` and inherited via role hierarchies. Index-level permissions only gate which indexes a role can search/write. The UI inactivity timeout governs idle session expiry, not action permission. App visibility flags only affect which apps appear in the UI, not what a user is allowed to do.

questions.question: A Splunk admin needs a near-real-time, browser-based view of overall environment health — indexer queues filling up, forwarder connection counts, search concurrency, and license usage. Which built-in app should they open?
questions.explanation: The Monitoring Console (MC, historically called the Distributed Management Console — DMC) is the built-in admin app that aggregates platform health metrics: indexer pipeline queues, indexing rate, forwarder connections, search-head load, license usage, KV store and clustering status. Enterprise Security and ITSI are paid premium apps focused on security analytics and service-level monitoring respectively. Splunk Stream is a wire-data capture add-on.

questions.question: In an indexer cluster, an administrator sets replication factor (RF) = 3 and search factor (SF) = 2. What does SF = 2 specifically guarantee?
options: Two of the copies include the searchable index files (tsidx), so search can continue if one searchable copy is lost.
Three copies of raw data exist but none are searchable.
The cluster keeps two indexers online at all times.
Data is retained for two years before rolling to frozen.
questions.explanation: Search factor is the number of copies that include the searchable tsidx index files; SF = 2 means two of the RF = 3 raw copies are also searchable, so the cluster can lose one searchable copy and still serve searches without rebuilding. RF controls total raw copies (3 here), not searchability; SF is not a count of online indexers or a retention period.

questions.question: A universal forwarder must send data to indexers, but the admin wants to centrally manage which apps/config the forwarders receive. Which Splunk component distributes that configuration?
options: The deployment server, which pushes apps to deployment clients grouped by serverclass.
questions.explanation: The deployment server centrally manages forwarder (deployment-client) configuration, pushing apps to clients matched by serverclass rules. The license master enforces license usage, the deployer distributes config to search-head cluster members (not forwarders), and the monitoring console observes platform health — none manage forwarder app distribution.

questions.question: An admin needs a sourcetype's timestamps parsed correctly and events line-broken properly at index time. On which component and in which conf file do these parsing settings belong?
options: On the search head in savedsearches.conf.
On the universal forwarder in limits.conf.
On the indexer (or heavy forwarder) in props.conf, since event breaking and timestamp extraction happen during index-time parsing.
On the license master in server.conf.
questions.explanation: Line breaking and timestamp recognition are index-time parsing operations, configured in props.conf on the component that parses the data — the indexer, or a heavy forwarder if parsing occurs there. savedsearches.conf defines scheduled searches, a universal forwarder does not parse (it forwards raw data) and limits.conf tunes limits, and server.conf/license master are unrelated to sourcetype parsing.

questions.question: Two apps define a conflicting setting for the same stanza. Given Splunk configuration precedence in a typical global context, which layer wins?
options: The app whose name comes first alphabetically, always, regardless of context.
Whichever app was installed most recently.
The setting with the longest value string.
Following the layering rules, more specific/local contexts and higher-priority directories override lower ones (e.g., local beats default, and system/local can override app settings).
questions.explanation: Splunk merges configuration by precedence: within an app, local overrides default, and across the system the context (global vs app vs user) and directory priority determine the winner (system/local is highest in global context). Alphabetical app-name ordering is only a tiebreaker within the same precedence level, not the primary rule; value length and install recency are irrelevant.

questions.question: A hot bucket has stopped receiving new data and meets a roll condition. What is the correct order of the bucket lifecycle stages?
options: hot → warm → cold → frozen (then optionally thawed)
questions.explanation: Data is written to a hot bucket; when it rolls it becomes warm, later moves to cold (typically cheaper storage) as it ages, and finally rolls to frozen where it is deleted or archived (archived frozen data can be thawed). The other orderings invert this aging path.

questions.question: An admin must route a subset of incoming events to a different index based on their content. Which two conf files work together to do this at parse time?
options: props.conf (to apply a TRANSFORMS class to the sourcetype) and transforms.conf (to define the regex and destination index).
questions.explanation: Index-time routing uses props.conf to attach a TRANSFORMS-<class> to the sourcetype/source/host, and transforms.conf to define the matching regex and the DEST_KEY/_MetaData:Index target — together they route matching events to another index at parse time. savedsearches/macros are search-time, inputs/outputs handle collection and forwarding destinations (not per-event index routing), and authorize/authentication govern access.

questions.question: A daily indexing volume exceeds the licensed quota several days in a row. What is the direct consequence in current Splunk Enterprise licensing, and the admin's best response?
options: Indexing stops immediately and data is lost; the admin must buy a new license that hour.
Splunk deletes the oldest index to make room.
A license violation warning is recorded; repeated violations can restrict search until resolved, so the admin should reduce ingestion or increase the license.
Nothing happens; license limits are advisory only with no effect.
questions.explanation: Exceeding the daily ingest quota logs a license violation warning; accumulating violations within the rolling window can restrict searching (indexing generally continues) until the situation is corrected, so the admin should trim ingestion or raise the license capacity. Splunk does not immediately stop indexing and lose data, does not delete indexes to make room, and license limits are enforced — not advisory.

questions.question: In a search head cluster, an admin must deploy a new app and its knowledge objects to all members consistently. Which component and workflow is correct?
options: Copy the app manually onto each search head and restart them one by one.
Place the app on an indexer and let it replicate to search heads.
Use the deployment server to push it as a serverclass.
Push the app from the deployer to the SHC members using the apply shcluster-bundle workflow.
questions.explanation: Search-head cluster apps and configuration are distributed by the deployer via `apply shcluster-bundle`, which replicates the app consistently to all members (the captain coordinates). Manual copying risks drift, the deployment server manages forwarders/other clients rather than SHC members, and indexers do not replicate apps to search heads.

questions.question: A user should be able to run searches but must not be allowed to delete data with the `| delete` command. How does an admin enforce this?
options: Assign a role whose capabilities exclude the delete capability (which is not granted by default), following least privilege.
Give the user the admin role so restrictions are clearer.
questions.explanation: Splunk authorization is capability-based: the ability to run `| delete` requires the special `delete` capability, which is not granted to standard roles by default — so assigning a role without that capability lets the user search but not delete. Granting admin over-privileges them, deleting the account or disabling search removes legitimate access they need.

questions.question: An admin wants a single built-in interface to monitor indexing rate, search performance, and resource usage across the deployment. Which Splunk tool is designed for this?
options: The Monitoring Console (formerly DMC), which provides platform health and performance views across roles.
The license master usage report only.
A third-party APM agent installed on each host.
questions.explanation: The Monitoring Console (formerly the Distributed Management Console) is Splunk's built-in tool for monitoring platform health — indexing throughput, search performance, resource usage, and per-role status across the deployment. The deployment server manages forwarder config, the license report covers only ingest volume, and a third-party APM is unnecessary for Splunk's own platform monitoring.
